introduction: These readings place the human being at the summit of creation. The world is a tree and man its fruit; the mineral, the plant and the animal are gathered up in him, and to them he adds the rational soul; without him the universe would be a body without a spirit; he is the mirror in which all the divine names can be reflected, and the fruit he is meant to bear is love and knowledge. Some passages argue against the view that the human species is an accident, or once was another kind. All seventy-one quotations are read here beside seventy-one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the eighth psalm, 'in our image', the Qur'an's 'best stature' and 'viceroy', Sophocles, Aristotle on reason and speech, Pascal's thinking reed, Rumi's ascent through the kingdoms, Pope's chain of being, Leibniz, Blake. Ten push back or add a side: the Preacher's 'no preeminence above a beast', Darwin twice, Nietzsche's 'much within you is still worm', Pascal's silent spaces and his 'nothing in comparison with the infinite', Hamlet's 'quintessence of dust', Aristotle on nature's gradual steps, Mencius on how small the human difference is and how easily lost, and Proverbs on what the righteous owe their animals.
questions: In what sense is the human being the 'fruit' of the tree of existence? What does the image imply about the rest of the tree?
The readings say the fruit of the human tree is love and knowledge. What follows for a life that bears neither?
Darwin saw a difference of degree between humans and other animals; the readings insist on a difference of kind. What is at stake in the choice?
Pascal was frightened by the silence of infinite space. Is the claim that the universe would be 'dead' without man an answer to him, or an example of what he feared losing?
If all things were created for man, what does man owe them? What does Proverbs suggest?
Mencius says most people throw away what makes them human. How is the station described here kept?

outside.why: Blake would see a world in a grain of sand, and a heaven in a wild flower.
Julian of Norwich was shown a little thing the size of a hazel-nut in her palm, and understood that it was all that is made.
Malachi asks: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?
Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit, and love comes first: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness.
Paul ends his chapter on love: now abideth faith, hope, charity; but the greatest of these is charity.
Jesus said: make the tree good and his fruit good, for the tree is known by his fruit.
A psalm asks what man is, and answers: thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory.
Genesis says: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
The Qur'an gives the purpose in a line: I created jinn and humankind only that they might worship me.
Mencius said that all things are already complete in us, and that there is no greater delight than sincerity.
Jesus told his followers: ye are the light of the world; a city set on an hill cannot be hid.
Genesis gives humankind dominion over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.
The Qur'an says God hath made of service unto you whatsoever is in the heavens and in the earth.
Proverbs says that a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast. If all was created for man, what does man owe to all?
George Herbert says that who sweeps a room as for God's laws makes the action fine.
Aristotle held that reason, more than anything else, is man, and the life of reason best for him.
Sophocles' chorus sings that wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man.
Pope placed man on an isthmus of a middle state, a being darkly wise, and rudely great.
Aristotle says that all men by nature desire to know, as their delight in the senses shows.
Leibniz called each simple substance a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Pope saw the kingdoms as one chain, in which to strike any link breaks the whole.
Darwin concluded that the difference in mind between man and the higher animals, great as it is, is one of degree and not of kind. Where do the readings place the break?
Aristotle says that man is the only animal endowed with the gift of speech, and so with a sense of just and unjust.
Pascal sought human dignity not in space, which swallows him, but in the government of his thought.
Genesis says that God breathed into man's nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul.
Whitman called himself an acme of things accomplished, and an encloser of things to be.
Proverbs says: wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom, and with all thy getting get understanding.
Rumi tells the ascent as his own: I died as mineral and became a plant, died as plant and rose to animal, died as animal and I was man.
Emerson put it in a line: striving to be man, the worm mounts through all the spires of form.
Tennyson asks man to move upward, working out the beast, and let the ape and tiger die.
Hamlet praises man, 'the paragon of animals', and then asks: what is this quintessence of dust? Can both judgments be true?
Jesus asked what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Ecclesiastes says that what befalls the sons of men befalls beasts, and man hath no preeminence above a beast. What answers the Preacher?
Proverbs calls the spirit of man the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts.
John's Gospel says that the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not.
Marcus Aurelius regarded the universe as one living being, with one substance and one soul.
Plato's Timaeus says the maker put intelligence in soul and soul in body, and the world became a living creature.
Pascal wrote: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me. Is the universe waiting for man, or indifferent to him?
Kant was filled with awe by two things: the starry heavens above, and the moral law within.
Jesus said: I am the vine, ye are the branches; he that abideth in me bringeth forth much fruit.
In the parable the owner comes three years seeking fruit on his fig tree.
The first psalm likens the just to a tree that brings forth fruit in its season.
Jesus describes growth by stages: first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn.
Darwin saw grandeur in life's endless forms evolved from so simple a beginning. The reading holds that man was always a distinct species: how far apart are the two accounts?
Tennyson looked to one far-off divine event to which the whole creation moves.
Aristotle observed that nature proceeds little by little from lifeless things to animal life, so that the line cannot be fixed. Are the kinds as changeless as the reading says?
A psalmist says: I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Protagoras, as Plato reports him, called man the measure of all things.
The Qur'an says the same of the human form in one short verse: surely We created man of the best stature.
Paul says we are many members in one body, and not all have the same office.
Pope advised: know then thyself, presume not God to scan; the proper study of mankind is man.
Paul says that beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image.
Blake wrote that mercy has a human heart, and love the human form divine.
The Qur'an says the trust was offered to the heavens, the earth and the hills, and man assumed it.
Peter writes of promises by which we might be partakers of the divine nature.
The Qur'an says that God taught Adam all the names, and then asked the angels to tell them.
John's Gospel says that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
The Qur'an says: We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves.
Mencius said that what distinguishes man from the lower animals is but small, and most people cast it away. Is human superiority a given, or something kept?
Nietzsche's Zarathustra says: ye have made your way from the worm to man, and much within you is still worm. Is man the goal of the ages, or a stage?
Whitman says that for him the nebula cohered to an orb and the long slow strata piled.
A psalm exclaims: O Lord, how manifold are thy works; the earth is full of thy riches.
Pascal asked what man is in nature: a nothing in comparison with the infinite, an all in comparison with the nothing. Is 'the consummation of the universe' one half of that sentence?
Ecclesiastes says that the thing that hath been is that which shall be.
In the Qur'an God tells the angels: I am about to place a viceroy in the earth.
Genesis says that God saw every thing that he had made, and behold, it was very good.
Pope surveyed a vast chain of being which from God began, through angel, man, beast and insect.
Paul says that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, the things God hath prepared for them that love him.
Paul told the Athenians that in God we live, and move, and have our being.
Jesus said: by their fruits ye shall know them; a good tree bringeth forth good fruit.
Hopkins wrote that Christ plays in ten thousand places, lovely in limbs and eyes not his.
